passage: I'm Pemba, and I share a room with my sister Dolma, so I saw most of it. For two nights her phone kept lighting up with the class group, where she and Anirban had been fighting about the debate team captaincy in front of everyone. Last night she sat on her bed for a long time, typing and deleting. Then she closed the group and opened a chat with just Anirban. I peeked. She wrote: "That went too far. Can we meet before assembly tomorrow, just us two?" She put the phone face down like it was hot. It buzzed a few minutes later. She read it and let out a long breath. This morning she left early. When she came home, she was humming. I don't know what they said. But the group chat has been quiet all day.

qa.q: What had Dolma and Anirban been fighting about in the class group?
qa.a: They had been fighting about the debate team captaincy.

qa.q: What might Dolma have been feeling when she put the phone face down?
qa.a: She seems nervous about the reply; putting it down "like it was hot" suggests she felt exposed after reaching out first.

qa.q: Why was moving the talk out of the group chat a useful turning point?
qa.a: Away from the class audience, neither had to perform or save face, so they could really talk and the fight lost its fuel.

qa.q: How might Anirban have felt getting a private message instead of another public reply?
qa.a: Anirban may have felt relieved and less on guard, since a private invitation does not need defending in front of everyone.

grounding: Shows a teen sending a short private message that moves a public quarrel out of the group chat and into a face-to-face talk.

subtype: Stage 6: Owning your part, not the whole [Response]
passage: Honestly, Didi, the fight wasn't even the hard part. You know me, your little sister never backs down. The hard part was the bench behind the library, when Ritu and I finally sat down alone. I'd rehearsed a whole speech about how she started it by posting that photo. But when I opened my mouth, I just said, "I'm sorry I told everyone about your failed audition. That was mean." I didn't add "but you posted the photo." I wanted to, so badly. Ritu stared at her shoes, then said, "Kalyani, I'm sorry about the photo. I knew you'd hate it." Nobody brought up who began it. The funny thing? The next day Mehr and the others stopped taking sides too. When we cooled down, the whole group cooled down.

For a week the under-16 team had been split: Hemant's lot on one side of the dressing room, Omkar's on the other, all because of a foul in practice and a lot of shouting after. On Thursday, before warm-up, Hemant walked over to Omkar at the water tank. I couldn't hear everything. I caught "I shouldn't have shoved you," and then, after a pause, Omkar saying, "I shouldn't have called you a cheat." Neither said "you first." They shook hands, a bit awkwardly. The strange part was the rest of us. By the end of drills, people were passing across the old line like it had never been there.

subtype: Stage 1: Spark over a small thing [Actor]
passage: Your grandfather Gurpreet was not always this patient, Madhuri. At twenty-one I shared two rooms in Ludhiana with a boy called Satnam, both of us new at the textile mill. Every evening I came home to his tea glasses on the floor and his socks on my chair. Third day in a row, I picked up a glass and said, very sweetly, "Thank you, Satnam ji, for decorating our home." He laughed. I didn't. Later, lying awake, I understood it had nothing to do with glasses. I had been cooking for both of us for a month, and he had never once said it was good. I felt like a servant, not a friend. That is what the remark was really about. So when you complain about your flatmate's dishes, ask yourself what you are actually hungry for.

qa.a: He shared two rooms in Ludhiana with Satnam, both new at the textile mill.

qa.a: To ask what one is actually hungry for, meaning the need underneath the complaint, before speaking.

qa.a: Satnam probably heard only a joke about glasses and had no idea about the month of unthanked cooking building up underneath.

passage:
Warden's note, Block C, Room 14. Rukmini Iyer, 7 March.
Heard raised voices at 10 pm and went up. Sujay, pointing at the bins, had said that Kamal "never does anything around here." Kamal did not answer about the bins. Instead he listed, fast and loud: he had paid for the gas cylinder, fixed the fan, cleaned the bathroom twice last week, carried Sujay's parcel up four floors. His hands were shaking. Every item was a defence, as if he were on trial. The bins were still full when I arrived. I asked both to sit. I said to Kamal, "It sounds like you felt called lazy." He nodded, jaw tight. To Sujay: "What do you need, specifically?" "Just the bins on Tuesdays." Plan: rota on the door by tomorrow. Will check in on Friday.

qa.q: What did Kamal say he had fixed?
qa.a: He said he had fixed the fan.

qa.q: Why did Kamal answer with a list instead of talking about the bins?
qa.a: He felt hurt at being called lazy, so, hands shaking, he defended himself with everything he had done instead of talking about the bins.

qa.q: How did Rukmini Iyer turn the trial back into a request?
qa.a: Rukmini named Kamal's hurt, "you felt called lazy", and asked Sujay for a specific need, which turned out to be only the bins on Tuesdays.

qa.q: What was it like for Sujay to hear a long list in reply?
qa.a: Sujay probably felt unheard, since the bins were never addressed and the complaint became a contest over who does more.

grounding: Shows a flatmate hearing a complaint as an attack on his character and answering with a defensive list, turning a request into a trial.

passage:
12 November, late.
Parul said it tonight, standing in the kitchen doorway: "Do you ever notice anything in this flat?" And I just went off. Not shouting exactly, but listing. I paid the internet bill. I called the plumber. I bought the rice last week, and the detergent. I took out the recycling on Sunday. I heard myself going on and on, like a lawyer. She had only asked about the milk going sour in the fridge. I didn't even answer that. I was too busy proving I'm not a useless flatmate. Maybe it's Mummy's old line, "my son never lifts a finger," still stuck in my head. Now it's 1 am and I feel stupid and also still annoyed. Why did one question feel like she was calling me a bad person?
— Harish

qa.q: What had Parul actually asked about?
qa.a: She had only asked about the milk going sour in the fridge.

qa.q: Why did one question feel so big to Harish?
qa.a: He heard it as being called a useless, bad flatmate, perhaps echoing Mummy's old line, so he rushed to defend himself.

qa.a: Parul may have felt confused and shut out, since a small question about sour milk turned into a trial she never meant to start.

grounding: Shows a young man answering a flatmate's small question with a defensive list, protecting his self-image instead of hearing the request.

passage: I'm Nasreen, the third person in the flat, and I was in the kitchen when it turned. Afreen and Jagdish had started on who ate whose leftover biryani. Five minutes later it wasn't about biryani. "You just don't care about anyone but yourself," Afreen said. Jagdish's face went hard. "And you think you're better than all of us because your parents pay your rent." "That's not—" "Don't even. I know what you think." Every time one of them said "that's not true", the other rolled their eyes as if it proved the point. I stood holding a spoon, watching them argue with people who weren't in the room: the Afreen in Jagdish's head, the Jagdish in Afreen's. I couldn't tell who was right. I'm not sure either of them was really listening.

qa.q: What did the argument start about?
qa.a: Afreen and Jagdish had started on who ate whose leftover biryani.

qa.q: What does each of them believe when the other says "that's not true"?
qa.a: Each is frustrated and certain their guess about the other's motives is fact, so the denial only seems like more proof.

qa.q: What could break the mind-reading at this stage?
qa.a: One of them could ask instead of tell, such as "Is that what you think I mean? What did you mean?", and Nasreen could suggest a pause.

qa.q: How is the argument affecting Nasreen?
qa.a: Nasreen feels stuck and helpless in the kitchen, holding a spoon, unable to tell who is right while the two talk past each other.

grounding: Shows two flatmates turning a small quarrel into sweeping claims about each other's motives, hearing every denial as proof.

subtype: Stage 4: Peak and point of no return [Actor]
passage: Ayesha, sit down, drink your tea. You're angry with your roommate, I can see it. Let me tell you something. When I was twenty, in the nursing hostel in Kochi, I had a best friend called Leelamma. We argued over a borrowed saree she had stained. It got hotter and hotter, and then I said it: "No wonder your father left, look how careless you are." I saw her face go white. My own face burned with shame the same second. I knew I had gone too far. Still, I was proud, and she was angry, and I walked out instead of taking it back. We didn't speak for two years. I'm Kavitha, fifty-four years old, and I still remember her face. Don't let one sentence cost you two years.

passage: The photocopy shop outside the tehsil office in Shahabad was hot by noon, and so was the argument. Devika had found the cash box two hundred short again, and Wasim had just used the word "careless" about her accounts. Her voice rose. His did too. Then Wasim stopped, put both hands flat on the counter, and said, "I'm too angry to say anything useful. Give me one hour. I'll be back at one o'clock and we'll finish this." He walked to the canal bank and sat under the peepal tree. Devika watched him go, arms folded, half expecting him to disappear till night the way her uncle always did. At five to one, his cycle bell rang outside. He came in with two cups of tea.

passage: The argument in the tiny Valencia flat began over the heating bill and slid quickly into everything else. Beatriz was pacing; Ivan felt his jaw lock and heard himself about to say something about her mother. He stopped. "Bea, I'm too angry to talk well. Can we pick this up in an hour? Seven o'clock. I'm just going for a walk." She threw up her hands. "Great, just leave." "I'm coming back. Seven." He went down to the seafront and walked until his shoulders dropped. At six fifty-five, the key turned in the lock. He had two oranges from the corner shop and a calmer voice. Beatriz, who had spent the hour rehearsing how abandoned she felt, found she didn't need the speech.

subtype: Stage 6: Repair and one concrete agreement [Response]
passage:
Friday, 11 pm.
Salma and I finally sat down after yesterday's blow-up about the kitchen. We made a rule before starting: you say the other person's point back first. It felt silly. Salma went first: "You're saying you feel like you're the only one who notices the mess, and it makes you feel used." That was exactly it. Then I had to do hers: "You're saying you get home at nine, exhausted, and my nagging makes the flat feel like a second office." She nodded. I also said sorry for calling her lazy, which was the worst thing I said. She said sorry for "control freak". Then we wrote a rota on the back of an electricity bill and stuck it on the fridge. Mine: Mondays and Thursdays. Small. But it's on paper.
— Kiran

Counsellor's note, student wellbeing centre, 3 October.
Disha (20) booked the session for exam stress but spent most of it talking about her girlfriend, Mehak. Observations: she checked her phone four times. She described asking Mehak "Are we okay?" several times this week, and dropping hints like "Must be nice to have so much free time." She said she sounded sharper than she meant to, "like a tax officer". When I asked what she was afraid of, she was quiet, then said, "That one day she'll just stop replying." Her shoulders dropped as she said it. I reflected that the questions and hints seem to come from fear of being left rather than anger. Next step: she will try one direct sentence with Mehak, "I miss you and I'm worried about us." Follow-up in two weeks.

Sunday night.
Gurpreet left after lunch and I've felt weird all evening. He was on his phone half the time, laughing at something he didn't show me. I asked, "Everything okay with us?" He said, "Obviously, Madhu. You're my girl. Why?" Then I asked again while he was putting on his shoes. He sighed. And as he left I said, "Say hi to your very interesting phone." I heard how it sounded. Snippy. Not me. What I actually wanted to say was: I feel like you're drifting, and I'm scared I'm not enough anymore. Why can't I just say that? Instead it leaks out sideways, in questions and little jabs. Tomorrow I'll try. Maybe.
— Madhuri

"Did you get my messages?"
"I was in the lab. My phone was in the locker."
"I sent six. Six, Bhupen. What is wrong with us?"
"Nothing's wrong. Can I just take my shoes off?"

She followed him into the kitchen. He opened the fridge and stared into it.

She was sure that if she just kept going, if he would only answer properly, they'd be close again.

passage:
Looking back at that semester, I can see what I was doing, even if I couldn't then. Pranav had gone quiet: his exams, his part-time job, his mother's surgery back home. And me? I was his girlfriend of eight months, and I texted. Good-morning texts, lunch texts, "are u free?" texts, then "why aren't you answering??" By evening I'd have sent ten. When he finally picked up, I'd start with "Are we breaking up or what?" before he'd said hello. I honestly believed that if I pushed hard enough, I'd break through to the Pranav who used to walk me home. Every silence felt like a door closing, so I knocked louder. It never once occurred to me that the knocking was what made him lock it.
— Vidya

qa.q: What would Vidya say when Pranav finally picked up?
qa.a: She'd start with "Are we breaking up or what?" before he'd said hello.

qa.q: What did Vidya believe pushing harder would achieve?
qa.a: She believed she would break through to the Pranav who used to walk her home, so every silence made her knock louder.

qa.q: Looking back, what might have been a better move for Vidya at that stage?
qa.a: She could have sent one warm message acknowledging his exams, job and his mother's surgery, then given him room to answer.

qa.q: How might Pranav have experienced ten texts a day during that semester?
qa.a: Already stretched by exams, work and his mother's surgery, Pranav probably felt swamped and pulled further away. 😔

grounding: Shows a young woman pursuing a withdrawn partner with more and more messages, sure that pressing harder is the only way to reach him.
